headline: We would have won in a landslide
dek: On the evening of the midterm elections, the President points out that he was not on the ballot, and says that if he had been, he would have won in a landslide.

original.speaker: Donald J. Trump
text: I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP
original.context: Posted on the evening of 3 November 2026, election day for the US midterm elections.

verification.note: Copied by the editor from truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump on 9 November 2026 (shown as Nov 03, 2026, 7:37 PM Pacific).

en: I was not a candidate in tonight’s elections, but our agenda was on the ballot in every state, and I remain confident that it has the support of a great many Americans.
I thank everyone who voted. Now the work continues, with the Congress the American people have chosen.
fr: Je n’étais pas candidat aux élections de ce soir, mais notre programme était soumis au vote dans chaque État, et je reste convaincu qu’il a le soutien d’un très grand nombre d’Américains.
Je remercie toutes celles et tous ceux qui ont voté. Le travail continue, avec le Congrès que les Américains ont choisi.

text: J’étais pas sur le bulletin. Et si j’y avais été, on aurait gagné, et pas qu’un peu : un raz-de-marée.

Bon, je dis ça, je dis rien. Chez nous on dit « y en a point comme nous », mais on le dit doucement, entre deux verres de chasselas, pas en majuscules. Alors disons qu’on aurait gagné… faut voir. Merci de votre attention, quand vous aurez un moment.
en: I wasn’t on the ballot. And if I had been, we’d have won, and not by a little: a landslide.

Well, I’m just saying, I’m not saying anything. Round here we say “there’s nobody like us”, but we say it quietly, between two glasses of Chasselas, not in capital letters. So let’s say we would have won… we’ll see. Thank you for your attention, whenever you have a moment.
notes: “Y en a point comme nous” (“there’s nobody like us”) is the Vaud motto of cheerful self-satisfaction; Chasselas is the white grape of the Lavaux vineyards. “Faut voir” (“we’ll see”) is the classic Vaudois non-answer.

text: Adieu ! J’étais pas sur le bulletin. Si j’y avais été, on gagnait par avalanche. Pas par glissement de terrain : par avalanche.

Ceux d’en bas peuvent bien voter ce qu’ils veulent. Chez nous, on monte voter à pied, on redescend pour la raclette, et le résultat, on le connaît avant même d’ouvrir l’urne. Merci de votre attention, et fermez la porte, vous laissez entrer le froid.
en: Adieu! I wasn’t on the ballot. If I had been, we’d have won by an avalanche. Not a landslide: an avalanche.

The people down in the lowlands can vote however they like. Up here we walk up to vote, walk back down for the raclette, and we know the result before the ballot box is even opened. Thank you for your attention, and shut the door, you’re letting the cold in.
notes: In Valais, “Adieu” means hello. “Ceux d’en bas” (“the people down below”) is how the Valais mountains speak of the rest of Switzerland. Raclette, cheese melted by the fire and scraped onto potatoes, comes from Valais. In French, a “glissement de terrain” is only a literal landslide; a landslide victory is a “raz-de-marée”.

text: J’étais même pas sur le bulletin. Et si j’y avais été, on gagnait par K.-O., direct, au premier tour.

Mais bon, voter, faut y aller : la ligne 13 est blindée, le bureau de vote est au fond d’une école, et l’assesseur te regarde comme si tu lui devais de l’argent. Moi, j’aurais gagné sans même me déplacer. Merci de votre attention, enfin, si vous avez cinq minutes, parce que moi je suis pressé.
en: I wasn’t even on the ballot. And if I had been, we’d have won by knockout, straight away, in the first round.

But hey, voting means actually going: the line 13 metro is packed, the polling station is at the back of a school, and the official at the table looks at you like you owe him money. Me, I’d have won without even leaving the house. Thank you for your attention, that is, if you’ve got five minutes, because I’m in a hurry.
notes: Line 13 is the Paris metro line Parisians most love to complain about. In France, polling stations are often in schools, and an election can be won outright “au premier tour”, in the first round.

text: J’étais pas sur le bulletin. Mais si j’y avais été, peuchère, on gagnait cent mille à zéro. Que dis-je : un million.

Les autres, ils faisaient Fanny, devant tout le monde, sur la place du village. Et je vous le dis sans exagérer, moi je n’exagère jamais : on en aurait parlé jusqu’à Marseille, et même jusqu’à Toulon. Merci pour votre attention, et ça, c’est pas une galéjade.
en: I wasn’t on the ballot. But if I had been, good heavens, we’d have won a hundred thousand to nil. What am I saying: a million.

The others would have had to kiss Fanny, in front of everybody, on the village square. And I tell you without exaggerating, I never exaggerate: they’d have talked about it all the way to Marseille, and even to Toulon. Thank you for your attention, and that’s no tall tale.
notes: At pétanque, a player who loses 13–0 “fait Fanny”: by tradition they must kiss the bottom of Fanny, a picture or statue of a bare-bottomed woman kept in the café. “Peuchère” is a Provençal exclamation; a “galéjade” is a tall tale.

text: I wasn’t even on the ballot. And if I had been, we would’ve won so big you’d need a bigger map. Texas-sized. Bigger than Texas, and I don’t say that lightly around here.
Folks, a landslide is for amateurs. We’d have won a stampede. Thank you kindly for your attention to this matter.
en: He points out he wasn’t a candidate, and says that if he had been, his victory would have been enormous: “Texas-sized”, the state’s favourite unit of measurement.
A landslide isn’t big enough for him: he wants a stampede, a cattle-country word for everyone charging in the same direction.

text: I wasn’t on the ballot. If I was, we’d have won in a landslide. A wicked big one. Bigger than the ’04 comeback.
And don’t give me the polls. This town was arguing about taxes before there was a country to vote in. Thanks for your attention, now get outta the way, I’m double-parked.
en: He says he would have won enormously (“wicked” means “very” in Boston) and compares it to 2004, when the Red Sox came back from three games down to beat the Yankees.
He waves away the polls, recalls that Boston was arguing about taxes before the United States existed (the Boston Tea Party, 1773), and leaves in a hurry: he’s double-parked.

text: I wasn’t even on the ballot. And if I had been, we’d have won in a landslide. A proper one, not a wee one.

Mind you, we know a thing or two about results up here. We gave the world the television you watched them on, and the telephone you’d have phoned to complain. Anyone who says I wouldn’t have won? Aye, right. Thanks for your attention to this matter.
en: He wasn’t a candidate, but says he would have won a “proper” landslide, not a “wee” (small) one.

He reminds everyone that Scots gave the world the television (John Logie Baird) and the telephone (Alexander Graham Bell, born in Edinburgh), and answers any doubters with “aye, right”: the famous Scottish double positive that means “no chance”.

text: His Majesty’s Government notes that the President was not a candidate in these elections, and that he has nonetheless taken a close interest in their outcome.
In our experience, hypothetical elections are the most reliably won. We wish the newly elected members of Congress every success.
en: He would like you to know he would have won anyway. Nobody can prove otherwise, which is rather the beauty of it.

text: France has followed these midterm elections with the greatest interest: they are a moment of democratic vitality for our oldest ally.

In France, too, the Constitution limits the President to two consecutive terms. We have learned that a leader’s legacy is measured less by the elections he imagines winning than by the institutions he leaves stronger behind him.
fr: La France a suivi ces élections de mi-mandat avec le plus grand intérêt : elles sont un moment de vitalité démocratique chez notre plus vieil allié.

Chez nous aussi, la Constitution limite le Président à deux mandats consécutifs. Nous avons appris que l’héritage d’un dirigeant se mesure moins aux élections qu’il imagine gagner qu’aux institutions qu’il laisse plus fortes derrière lui.
notes: France has been America’s ally since the treaty of 1778. Since the constitutional revision of 2008, a French President may serve no more than two consecutive terms.

text: The Federal Council takes note of these elections.

In Switzerland, the members of the Federal Council are never on a ballot: they are elected by Parliament. The people, meanwhile, vote on the issues themselves, several times a year. Landslides are rare; we find this restful.
fr: Le Conseil fédéral prend acte de ces élections.

En Suisse, les membres du Conseil fédéral ne figurent jamais sur un bulletin : ils sont élus par le Parlement. Le peuple, lui, vote directement sur les sujets, plusieurs fois par an. Les raz-de-marée y sont rares ; nous trouvons cela reposant.
notes: The seven members of the Swiss Federal Council are elected by the Federal Assembly; Swiss citizens vote on federal popular votes up to four times a year.
